Customer Insights – A Statistical Investigation¶

Objective¶

This project analyzes customer demographics, spending behavior, engagement patterns, and demographic influences using statistical methods.

Business Goals¶

  • Understand customer demographics
  • Analyze spending behavior
  • Identify customer segments
  • Perform hypothesis testing
  • Generate business insights

Dataset: US_Customer_Insights_Dataset.csv

Statistical Summary Insights¶

The table highlights key descriptive statistics for customer attributes:

  • Age

    • Average age is ~49 years, with a median close to 49, indicating a fairly symmetric distribution.
    • Standard deviation of ~18 suggests a wide spread across age groups, useful for segmentation.

  • Monthly Spend

    • Mean spend (₹332) is higher than the median (~₹282), hinting at right-skewed behavior — a few high-spending customers are pulling the average up.
    • High variability (Std Dev ~226) shows spending patterns differ significantly across customers.

  • Days Since Last Interaction

    • Average of ~538 days with a median of 445 indicates many customers have not engaged recently.
    • Large spread (Std Dev ~399) suggests inconsistent engagement cycles, pointing to potential churn risk.

** Analyst Takeaway:**

  • Spending distribution is skewed — focus on identifying and nurturing high-value customers.
  • Engagement gaps are significant — reactivation campaigns could reduce churn.
  • Age diversity supports tailored marketing strategies across segments.

In [6]:
plt.figure(figsize=(9,6))

# Histogram with custom colors and transparency
sns.histplot(df['Age'], bins=20, kde=True, 
             color="skyblue", edgecolor="black", alpha=0.7)

# Overlay KDE with bold contrasting color
sns.kdeplot(df['Age'], color="red", linewidth=2)

# Titles and labels with styling
plt.title(" Age Distribution of Customers ", fontsize=16, fontweight="bold", color="darkblue")
plt.xlabel("Age", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
plt.ylabel("Frequency", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")

# Add gridlines for readability
plt.grid(axis="y", linestyle="--", alpha=0.6)

# Highlight mean with vertical line
plt.axvline(df['Age'].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label=f"Mean: {df['Age'].mean():.1f}")

# Highlight median with vertical line
plt.axvline(df['Age'].median(), color="purple", linestyle=":", linewidth=2, label=f"Median: {df['Age'].median():.1f}")

# Add legend
plt.legend()

plt.show()

Age Distribution Insights¶

The histogram shows how customer ages are spread across the dataset:

  • Central Tendency

    • Mean age ≈ 49.5 years
    • Median age ≈ 49.0 years
    • The closeness of mean and median indicates a fairly balanced distribution without strong skew.

  • Spread

    • Ages range widely (approx. 10–90 years), reflecting diverse demographics.
    • The distribution is concentrated around middle age, with fewer customers at the extremes.

  • Business Implications

    • Middle-aged customers form the core segment — marketing strategies should prioritize this group.
    • Younger and older age brackets are smaller but may represent niche opportunities (e.g., youth-focused offers or senior benefits).
    • Balanced distribution suggests segmentation by age bands could yield actionable insights for personalization.

Analyst Takeaway:
The customer base is centered around middle age, with meaningful representation across other age groups. Tailored campaigns by age segment can maximize engagement and improve targeting efficiency.

Monthly Spend Distribution Insights¶

The histogram reveals how customers differ in their monthly spending:

  • Central Tendency

    • Mean spend = USD 331.6
    • Median spend = USD 282.1
    • The mean is noticeably higher than the median, indicating a right-skewed distribution — a few high-spending customers are pulling the average upward.

  • Spread

    • Most customers spend between $0–$500, with a peak around $200–$250.
    • A smaller group spends significantly more, creating a long tail in the distribution.

  • Business Implications

    • Majority of customers are low-to-mid spenders, forming the core revenue base.
    • High-spending customers, though fewer, contribute disproportionately to overall revenue — they represent a premium segment worth nurturing.
    • Skewness suggests opportunities for tiered loyalty programs or differentiated offers to maximize value across segments.

Analyst Takeaway:
Customer spending is uneven, with a strong base of moderate spenders and a small but impactful premium group. Strategies should balance retention of the majority while investing in personalized engagement for high-value customers.

# Age Distribution — Boxplot
plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))
sns.boxplot(y=df['Age'])

plt.title("Age Boxplot")
plt.show()

Age Distribution — Boxplot Analysis¶

The boxplot provides a clear summary of the Age variable:

  • Median Age (~50 years): The central line indicates that half of the population is younger than 50, while the other half is older.
  • Interquartile Range (IQR ~35–65 years): Most individuals fall within this middle spread, showing the typical age range of the dataset.
  • Whiskers (~18–80 years): These extend to the minimum and maximum non-outlier values, highlighting the broader age span.
  • Outliers: Any points beyond the whiskers suggest unusually young or old individuals compared to the majority.

Business Insight:
The age distribution is fairly balanced around middle age, with a wide spread across younger and older groups. This indicates potential for segmentation strategies—for example, tailoring products or services differently for younger (<35), middle-aged (35–65), and senior (>65) customers.

Monthly Spend — Boxplot Insight¶

The boxplot provides a clear overview of customer spending behavior:

  • Median Spend (~300): Indicates that half of the customers spend below USD 300 monthly, while the other half spend more.
  • IQR (Interquartile Range <500): Most customers fall within this range, showing a concentrated spending pattern among the majority.
  • Outliers (up to ~1750): A few customers spend significantly higher amounts, representing premium or high-value segments.
  • Distribution Shape: The presence of multiple outliers and a long upper whisker suggests a right-skewed distribution, meaning a small group drives higher revenue.

Analytical Insight:
The spending pattern reveals that while most customers are moderate spenders, a small elite group contributes disproportionately to total revenue. This insight can guide customer segmentation and targeted marketing strategies—for instance, designing loyalty programs for high spenders and affordability campaigns for the majority.

Gender Distribution — Analytical Insight¶

The bar chart highlights the composition of customers across gender categories:

  • Male (~3700): Largest segment, slightly higher than other groups.
  • Non-Binary (~3500): Strong representation, nearly equal to female counts.
  • Female (~3400): Slightly lower but still a significant proportion.

Key Observations:

Business Insight:
Marketing and engagement strategies should remain inclusive and diversified, ensuring equal representation across all gender identities. Since the distribution is balanced, campaigns can focus more on behavioral or spending patterns rather than relying solely on gender segmentation.

Education Distribution — Analytical Insight¶

The dataset shows the following proportions of customer education levels:

  • Master (21.26%) → Largest segment, indicating a strong presence of highly educated individuals.
  • Associate (20.17%) & Bachelor (19.93%) → Together form nearly 40% of the base, representing mid-level education groups.
  • High School (19.86%) → Comparable to Bachelor, showing balanced representation of foundational education.
  • PhD (18.79%) → Smallest group, but still significant, highlighting advanced academic achievers.

Key Observations:

  • The distribution is fairly balanced across all categories, with no extreme dominance.
  • A slight skew toward Master’s degree holders suggests a customer base with higher education attainment.
  • The presence of substantial PhD and High School segments indicates diversity in educational backgrounds.

Business Insight:
Educational diversity implies varied preferences and decision-making behaviors.

  • Master/PhD holders may respond well to premium, knowledge-driven offerings.
  • Associate/Bachelor groups represent the mainstream, ideal for broad marketing campaigns.
  • High School segment may prefer affordable and practical solutions.

Top 10 States — Customer Distribution Insight¶

The chart highlights the states with the highest customer representation:

  • California (1180) → Largest customer base, a key market for targeted campaigns.
  • Florida (1152) & Ohio (1145) → Strong presence, nearly equal to California, forming secondary hubs.
  • Arizona (1087), New York (1085), Georgia (1080) → Mid-tier states with consistent customer counts.

Key Observations:

  • The distribution is fairly balanced, with most top states contributing ~900–1200 customers.
  • California leads, but the margin over Florida and Ohio is small, suggesting multiple strong markets rather than a single dominant one.
  • The spread across diverse regions (West, South, Midwest, East) indicates broad geographic coverage.

Business Insight:

  • Focus marketing and customer engagement strategies on California, Florida, and Ohio as primary growth drivers.
  • Maintain strong regional campaigns in Arizona, New York, and Georgia to leverage mid-tier markets.
  • Explore opportunities to boost presence in Illinois and Texas, where customer counts are slightly lower but still significant.

Correlation between Age and Monthly Spend: -0.01

Age vs Monthly Spend — Analytical Insight¶

The scatter plot explores the relationship between customer age and monthly spending:

  • Correlation (-0.01): The near-zero value indicates no meaningful relationship between age and spending.
  • Trend Line: The regression line is almost flat, confirming that spending patterns are independent of age.
  • Data Spread: Spending values are widely distributed across all age groups, with both younger and older customers showing similar variability.
  • Outliers: High spenders appear across different ages, suggesting that premium customers are not concentrated in any specific age bracket.

Key Observations:

  • Age does not drive monthly spending behavior — customers of all ages exhibit similar spending ranges.
  • High-value customers are scattered across age groups, meaning age-based segmentation alone is insufficient for targeting premium spenders.

Business Insight:
Marketing strategies should focus on behavioral and transactional attributes (e.g., spending habits, frequency of interaction, loyalty) rather than age demographics. Premium offers can be designed for high spenders across all age groups, while affordability campaigns can target the broader base without age bias.

Spending Behavior by Marital Status — Analytical Insight¶

The KDE plot compares monthly spending patterns between married and non-married customers:

  • Average Spend:

    • Married → USD332.35
    • Not Married → USD330.94
      The averages are nearly identical, showing no significant difference in spending behavior.

  • Distribution Shape: Both groups peak around USD250 monthly spend, with similar spread and tapering at higher values.

  • Overlap: The curves overlap almost entirely, indicating that marital status does not strongly influence spending.

Key Observations:

  • Spending behavior is consistent across marital status groups.
  • High spenders exist in both categories, suggesting premium customers are not concentrated in one group.
  • Marital status is not a strong predictor of monthly spend.

Business Insight:
Segmentation strategies should focus on behavioral and transactional attributes (e.g., frequency of purchases, loyalty, product categories) rather than marital status. Campaigns can be designed inclusively, ensuring both married and non-married customers are targeted with similar offers, while premium strategies should identify high spenders across both groups.

# Correlation Matrix Heatmap
# Compute correlation matrix
corr = df[['Age','NumPets','MonthlySpend','DaysSinceLastInteraction']].corr()

# Set modern style
sns.set_style("white")
plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))

# Create heatmap with enhancements
ax = sns.heatmap(
    corr,
    annot=True,              # show correlation values
    fmt=".2f",               # format values to 2 decimals
    cmap="RdYlBu",           # vibrant diverging colormap
    center=0,                # center around zero
    linewidths=0.5,          # grid lines between cells
    cbar_kws={"shrink":0.8, "label":"Correlation"}
)

# Title styling
plt.title("Correlation Matrix — Key Variables", fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', color="#003366", pad=15)

# Optional polish
plt.gca().set_facecolor("#F7FBFF")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Correlation Matrix — Analytical Insight¶

The matrix explores relationships among four key variables: Age, NumPets, Monthly Spend, and Days Since Last Interaction.

  • Age vs Monthly Spend (-0.01): No meaningful correlation; spending is independent of age.
  • Age vs NumPets (-0.02): Negligible relationship; pet ownership does not vary with age.
  • NumPets vs Monthly Spend (0.02): Very weak positive correlation; owning more pets does not significantly increase spending.
  • NumPets vs Days Since Last Interaction (-0.06): Slight negative correlation; customers with more pets may interact marginally more frequently.
  • Monthly Spend vs Days Since Last Interaction (0.01): No significant relationship; spending is not tied to recency of interaction.

Key Observations:

  • All correlations are close to zero, indicating that these variables are largely independent.
  • No strong linear relationships exist, meaning predictive models should not rely on these variables alone.
  • Behavioral and transactional features (e.g., frequency of purchases, product categories) may provide stronger signals than demographic attributes.

Business Insight:
Since demographic factors (age, pets) and interaction recency show minimal correlation with spending, segmentation strategies should focus on behavioral drivers. Advanced techniques like clustering or RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) analysis may yield more actionable insights than relying on simple correlations.

  • Non-Binary:

    • Not Married → 1894
    • Married → 1577
      Noticeable difference, with more individuals identifying as non-binary being unmarried.

Key Observations:

  • Males show the most balanced split between married and unmarried.
  • Females and Non-Binary groups lean toward being unmarried, though the difference is not extreme.
  • Overall, marital status distribution is relatively balanced across genders, with no overwhelming skew.

Business Insight:
Marital status does not drastically differ across genders, but slight variations exist.

  • Campaigns targeting family-oriented products/services may resonate more with married males.
  • Lifestyle or independent offerings could be positioned toward unmarried females and non-binary customers.
  • Inclusive strategies should ensure messaging reflects both married and unmarried segments across all genders.

Step 5 & 6: Hypothesis Testing¶

Decision Rule:

  • p-value < 0.05 → Reject H₀
  • p-value ≥ 0.05 → Fail to Reject H₀
In [3]:
# Hypothesis 1: Gender vs Monthly Spend
male = df[df['Gender']=="Male"]['MonthlySpend']
female = df[df['Gender']=="Female"]['MonthlySpend']

t_stat, p_value = ttest_ind(male, female)

print("T Statistic:", t_stat)
print("P Value:", p_value)

T Statistic: 0.3391730320232445
P Value: 0.7344892727022859

Hypothesis 1: Gender vs Monthly Spend¶

H₀: Male and Female customers spend the same.

H₁: Male and Female customers spend differently.

We conducted a two-sample t-test to compare average monthly spending between male and female customers.

  • Test Statistic (t): 0.34
  • p-value: 0.73

Interpretation:

  • Since the p-value (0.73) is greater than 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis (H₀).
  • This indicates that there is no statistically significant difference in monthly spending between male and female customers.
  • In practical terms, gender does not appear to be a key driver of spending behavior in this dataset.

Business Implication:
Marketing or segmentation strategies should not rely solely on gender-based assumptions for spending patterns. Instead, other factors such as income level, age group, or customer segment may provide stronger insights into spending differences.

In [5]:
# Hypothesis 2: Education vs Monthly Spend
groups = [
    x["MonthlySpend"].values
    for _, x in df.groupby("Education")
]

f_stat, p_value = f_oneway(*groups)

print("F Statistic:", f_stat)
print("P Value:", p_value)

F Statistic: 0.2288066867370917
P Value: 0.922359467759936

Hypothesis 2: Education vs Monthly Spend¶

H₀: Average spending is equal across education levels.

H₁: At least one education level has different spending.

We performed a one-way ANOVA to test whether average monthly spending differs across education levels.

  • F Statistic: 0.23
  • p-value: 0.92

Interpretation:

  • Since the p-value (0.92) is much greater than 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis (H₀).
  • This means there is no statistically significant difference in monthly spending across different education levels.
  • In other words, education level does not appear to influence spending behavior in this dataset.

Business Implication:
Customer education level is not a strong predictor of spending patterns. Marketing and segmentation strategies should instead focus on other variables (e.g., income, age, or lifestyle factors) that may provide more meaningful insights into spending behavior.

# Hypothesis 3: Marital Status vs Pet Ownership
contingency_table = pd.crosstab(
    df['Married'],
    df['NumPets']
)

chi2, p_value, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(contingency_table)

print("Chi Square:", chi2)
print("P Value:", p_value)

Chi Square: 177.63953668537033
P Value: 2.3957232932397494e-37

Hypothesis 3: Marital Status vs Pet Ownership¶

H₀: Marital status and pet ownership are independent.

H₁: Marital status and pet ownership are related.

We conducted a Chi-Square test of independence to examine whether marital status is related to pet ownership.

  • Chi-Square Statistic: 177.64
  • p-value: 2.40e-37

Interpretation:

  • The p-value is far below 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis (H₀).
  • This indicates a strong, statistically significant relationship between marital status and pet ownership.
  • In other words, pet ownership patterns vary meaningfully depending on whether a customer is married or not.

Business Implication:
Marital status can be a valuable segmentation factor for campaigns related to pet products or services. For example:

  • Married customers may show different preferences in pet ownership compared to single customers.
  • Tailored offers (e.g., family-oriented pet care packages vs. individual pet owner deals) could improve engagement and conversion.

# Hypothesis 4: Age vs Inactivity
corr, p_value = pearsonr(
    df['Age'],
    df['DaysSinceLastInteraction']
)

print("Correlation:", corr)
print("P Value:", p_value)

Correlation: -0.003970230104955041
P Value: 0.6816905437300954

Hypothesis 4: Age vs Inactivity¶

H₀: Age and inactivity are not related.

H₁: Age and inactivity are related.

We performed a Pearson correlation test to examine whether age is related to customer inactivity (measured as days since last interaction).

  • Correlation Coefficient (r): -0.004
  • p-value: 0.68

Interpretation:

  • The correlation is very close to zero, indicating no meaningful linear relationship between age and inactivity.
  • Since the p-value (0.68) is greater than 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis (H₀).
  • This suggests that age does not significantly influence how long customers remain inactive.

Business Implication:
Age is not a reliable predictor of customer inactivity. Retention strategies should instead focus on behavioral or transactional factors (e.g., purchase frequency, engagement with campaigns, or loyalty program participation) rather than demographic age groups.

Step 7: Business Insights¶

Customer Insights – A Statistical Investigation¶

Key Findings from Hypothesis Testing¶

  1. Gender vs Monthly Spend

    • No significant difference in spending between male and female customers.
    • 👉 Gender is not a strong driver of spending behavior.

  2. Education vs Monthly Spend

    • No significant difference in spending across education levels.
    • 👉 Education level does not influence spending patterns.

  3. Marital Status vs Pet Ownership

    • Strong, statistically significant relationship found.
    • 👉 Marital status is a valuable segmentation factor for pet-related products/services.

  4. Age vs Inactivity (Days Since Last Interaction)

    • No meaningful correlation between age and inactivity.
    • 👉 Age is not a predictor of customer engagement or retention.

  5. State vs Monthly Spend

    • No significant difference in spending across states.
    • 👉 Geographic state is not a key driver of spending behavior.

Business Insights¶

  • Demographics like gender, education, age, and state do not significantly impact spending or engagement.
  • Marital status shows strong influence on pet ownership, making it a useful segmentation variable for targeted campaigns.
  • Behavioral and transactional factors (purchase frequency, loyalty program participation, engagement with campaigns) are likely stronger predictors of customer value.
  • Marketing strategies should shift focus from broad demographics to behavioral segmentation for better targeting and retention.
  • For pet-related products, marital status segmentation can unlock differentiated offers (e.g., family-oriented vs individual pet owner campaigns).

Strategic Takeaway¶

Customer behavior is better explained by lifestyle and engagement patterns than by traditional demographics.
Invest in behavioral analytics and personalized campaigns to drive retention and revenue growth.

Objective¶

Analyze customer demographics, spending behavior, engagement patterns, and demographic influences using statistical methods.

Key Hypothesis Results¶

  • Gender vs Monthly Spend → ❌ No significant difference
  • Education vs Monthly Spend → ❌ No significant difference
  • Marital Status vs Pet Ownership → ✅ Strong, significant relationship
  • Age vs Inactivity → ❌ No meaningful correlation
  • State vs Monthly Spend → ❌ No significant difference

Business Insights¶

  1. Demographics (gender, education, age, state)

    • Do not significantly impact spending or engagement.
    • 👉 Traditional demographic segmentation is weak.

  2. Marital Status & Pet Ownership

    • Strong relationship detected.
    • 👉 Valuable segmentation factor for pet-related campaigns.

  3. Behavioral & Transactional Factors

    • Likely stronger predictors of customer value.
    • 👉 Focus on purchase frequency, loyalty program participation, and campaign engagement.

Strategic Takeaways¶

  • Shift marketing focus from broad demographics to behavioral segmentation.
  • Use marital status for targeted pet product/service campaigns.
  • Invest in personalized engagement strategies to improve retention and revenue.
  • Build dashboards that highlight behavioral drivers rather than static demographics.

Executive Summary¶

Customer behavior is better explained by lifestyle and engagement patterns than by demographics.
👉 To maximize ROI, prioritize behavioral analytics, loyalty tracking, and personalized campaigns over traditional demographic segmentation.
